seg.fce641038ff4.en: Shell and devein the prawns, rinse them well and drain in a colander.

seg.152d1d89f6a5.en: Rub the prawns with half the turmeric and a little salt; set aside 10 minutes. Use ¼ tsp turmeric and ¼ tsp of the salt.

seg.9e027c56020d.en: Heat the oil in a heavy kadai on medium heat and add the mustard seeds. When they splutter, add the green chillies and curry leaves.

seg.5d608fabeb97.en: Fry the onions in the oil till golden, then the ginger-garlic paste till it smells cooked. The onions take about 8–10 minutes; the paste about 1 minute, until the raw smell goes.

seg.7677bdc79559.en: If using the tomato, add it now and cook until soft and pulpy, about 4 minutes.

seg.5aff56b73c8a.en: Turn the heat to low. Add the rest of the turmeric, Teja chilli powder and coriander powder; fry 1 minute. Add the remaining salt and stir so the spices do not catch.

seg.ba25fbb9cf98.en: Pour in the water and cook the masala on medium heat until the oil starts to separate at the edges, about 3–4 minutes.

seg.e60a6389cdf2.en: Add the prawns and cook till they curl and turn pink, 5–6 minutes. Finish with garam masala. Stir often on medium-high heat so the masala dries and coats the prawns.

seg.af87e48d1429.en: Check doneness: prawns are cooked when they are pink and opaque all the way through and curled into a loose C. Cut one open if unsure; there should be no grey, see-through centre.

seg.32e58c09609e.en: Taste for salt, scatter the coriander leaves and switch off. Do not keep cooking once the prawns are done, or they turn rubbery.

seg.89a9cb293875.en: Teja is very hot: 1½ tsp makes a fiery iguru the way coastal homes like it; use 1 tsp for medium heat, or ½ tsp for mild.

seg.095c6105ce36.en: Fry the onions until properly golden; the colour and body of an iguru come from well-browned onions.

seg.04fb6307d058.en: Prawns cook fast. A loose C shape means done; a tight O means overcooked and chewy.

seg.a5e6a832090a.en: Pat the prawns dry after rinsing so they fry in the masala instead of stewing in water.

seg.4145e1ca56b5.en: Gongura royyalu: stir in ½ cup gongura leaves, wilted in a little oil and mashed, with the prawns.

seg.e52b316e5c51.en: Coconut: add 2 tbsp grated coconut or 3 tbsp thick coconut milk in the last 2 minutes for a softer, richer masala.

seg.fc55c7b1a788.en: Gravy style: add ¾ cup water after the prawns for a thinner royyala kura to pour over rice.

seg.8ccb6d545dd0.en: Serve hot with steamed rice and a spoon of ghee, or with rasam or sambar rice. It also goes well with chapati.

seg.e7cb15cc47e2.en: Keep leftovers covered in the fridge and eat within 1 day. Reheat in a pan only until steaming hot all the way through; longer reheating makes the prawns tough.

seg.8381d6ac4e4f.en: How do I know when prawns are cooked?

seg.45cd36ecb77b.en: They turn pink and opaque all the way through and curl into a loose C shape, usually in 5–6 minutes in the hot masala. A grey, see-through centre means they need a little longer.

seg.2e4c4a4632d7.en: What is the difference between iguru and vepudu?

seg.1ee73f38a967.en: Iguru is cooked down in an onion masala until thick and almost dry, with the masala clinging to the prawns. Vepudu is a fry, with less or no onion gravy, cooked until the prawns are crisp at the edges.

seg.d248a2970455.en: How can I make royyala iguru less spicy?

seg.8c9c12b68361.en: Use 1 tsp Teja chilli powder for medium heat or ½ tsp for mild, and skip the green chillies. A tablespoon of curd or coconut milk at the end also softens the heat.

seg.9cd9740c2604.en: Yes. Thaw them in the fridge, drain them well and pat them dry before rubbing with turmeric and salt. Frozen prawns release more water, so cook the masala a little longer.

seg.965a1e93fb08.en: Sunnundalu are the urad dal laddus of Andhra: split urad dal roasted till nutty, ground fine with jaggery and pressed together with hot ghee. There is no cooking of syrup, so they come together in about half an hour. Andhra homes make a tin for Sankranti and Diwali, pack them for relatives travelling abroad, and keep them for an evening sweet with tea.

seg.e564344550cd.en: Our Thati Bellam palm jaggery gives sunnundalu a deep brown colour and a rich, slightly smoky sweetness that suits the roasted dal. This recipe makes about 15 laddus.

seg.99983266b588.en: Pick through the urad dal for any small stones. Do not wash it; it must stay dry for roasting.

seg.2f2807ce216b.en: Put the dal in a heavy pan on a low flame.

seg.65588a76c883.en: Dry-roast the urad dal on a low flame till golden and nutty, about 10 minutes. Stir all the time so every grain colours evenly; it should smell toasty and snap when you bite a grain.

seg.9e8dc23d38fa.en: Tip the dal onto a plate and spread it out. Cool it, then grind to a fine powder. Grind in short bursts so the mixer does not heat up, and sieve out any coarse bits to grind again.

seg.edfa5bb66e59.en: Grate the palm jaggery finely, or pound the pieces in a mortar, breaking up any hard lumps.

seg.fcf7bce21bc5.en: Add the jaggery and cardamom powder to the dal powder in the mixer jar. Grind in the jaggery and cardamom till evenly mixed. A few pulses are enough; tip it all into a wide bowl.

seg.1cd01dc31b1a.en: Melt the ghee in a small pan until it is hot but not smoking.

seg.0b0ec921a239.en: Pour in the hot ghee, mix well and press into small balls. Start with most of the ghee, mix with a spoon, then use your hands once it is cool enough to touch.

seg.0c005163369c.en: Take a small handful and squeeze it firmly in your fist, then roll it round between your palms. If it crumbles, add a spoon more hot ghee to the bowl and mix.

seg.7ac27bb5fb12.en: Set the laddus on a plate to firm up for 15–20 minutes before storing.

seg.591b2b7e4ef4.en: Roast the dal on a low flame so it cooks through without burning.

seg.07daa833e53a.en: Grind the dal only after it has cooled completely; warm dal turns pasty in the mixer.

seg.33701abc66f0.en: Shape the laddus while the mixture is still warm; it binds best with the heat of the ghee.

seg.b6fb58b6b287.en: Palm jaggery pieces vary in hardness, so grate or pound them small before they go into the mixer.

seg.f95b0650add7.en: With skin: use black split urad dal with its skin for darker, grainier sunnundalu, the way some village homes make them.

seg.07498f6166e4.en: With sugar: use ¾ cup powdered sugar in place of the jaggery for pale, crisp-melting laddus.

seg.8fea3a4a695f.en: Serve as an evening sweet with tea or coffee, or as part of the Sankranti and Diwali sweet plate.

seg.83b4edc5c69d.en: Keep in an airtight steel tin at room temperature and eat within 2 weeks. In warm weather they keep longer in the fridge; let them come to room temperature before eating.

seg.c0ae9315eb0e.en: Why are my sunnundalu not holding shape?

seg.03c64235659e.en: The mixture needs more hot ghee, or it has cooled down. Warm a spoon or two of ghee, mix it in and shape the laddus while the mixture is still warm.

seg.ea5408ec0853.en: Can I make sunnundalu with cane jaggery?

seg.ec48010dffbe.en: Yes. Grate the cane jaggery (cheruku bellam) finely and use the same amount as palm jaggery. The laddus turn lighter in colour, with a milder, caramel-like sweetness.

seg.b2aed25ebff6.en: About 2 weeks in an airtight tin at room temperature, and longer in the fridge. Use a dry spoon or dry hands to take them out.

seg.e750875c4912.en: Should I use urad dal with or without skin?

seg.b12320430e22.en: Both are made in Andhra. White skinless urad dal gives smooth, light brown laddus; black urad dal with skin gives darker, grainier ones.

seg.02d0a5789a02.en: Tomato pachadi is the everyday chutney of Andhra kitchens: ripe tomatoes cooked down in oil with roasted dals, then ground coarse with chilli, garlic and a little tamarind. Many homes still grind it in the stone roti for a rough, spoonable texture, though a mixer in short pulses does the job. It goes with hot rice and ghee, dosa, idli and pesarattu.

seg.7735dff0ccd2.en: Our Sannam chilli powder gives it a deep red colour and steady, medium heat, and a little turmeric powder goes in with the tomatoes. This recipe makes about 1½ cups.

seg.2c1074e3a23e.en: Heat 2 tbsp oil in a kadai on medium-low heat.

seg.9d0674551be0.en: Fry the urad dal, chana dal and methi in oil till golden; lift them out. This takes 2–3 minutes; stir all the time, as methi burns fast and turns bitter.

seg.4727da6f2a95.en: In the same oil, add the chopped tomatoes and stir for a minute on medium heat.

seg.8032f2a2778c.en: Cook the tomatoes with turmeric and salt till soft and the juice dries up. Cover for the first 5 minutes, then cook uncovered, stirring now and then, about 12–15 minutes in all, until the tomatoes are pulpy and oil shows at the edges.

seg.d606b6ac13a2.en: Switch off, stir in the tamarind so it softens in the heat, and let everything cool for about 5 minutes.

seg.c1820dcae462.en: In the stone roti or a mixer jar, first grind the fried dals and methi to a coarse powder.

seg.f07d8b97d1db.en: Grind the dals, garlic, tamarind, chilli powder and tomatoes coarsely. In a mixer, add the garlic, chilli powder and cooked tomatoes to the dal powder and pulse 4–5 times without water; stop while it still has texture. Stir in the coriander leaves, if using.

seg.6675d75425f6.en: Taste and adjust: a pinch more salt, or a little more chilli powder pulsed in, if you want it hotter.

seg.27426b7ca3c6.en: Spoon the pachadi into a bowl. Heat 1 tbsp oil in a small pan and add the mustard seeds; when they splutter, add the urad dal and fry until golden.

seg.77131f9506c3.en: Add the red chillies, asafoetida and curry leaves and stir for a few seconds.

seg.d4a4b9439500.en: Temper with mustard, red chillies and curry leaves; pour over. Mix it in just before serving.

seg.0f23e6b9231e.en: Cook the tomatoes till the juice dries up so the pachadi keeps longer and does not taste raw.

seg.bad083b47507.en: Ripe, deep-red tomatoes give the best colour; if yours are sour, cut the tamarind to half.

seg.99bd4830d431.en: Pulse, do not run the mixer: a coarse pachadi is how Andhra homes like it, and a smooth paste loses that texture.

seg.27f2aaa2d25d.en: Sannam chilli powder gives medium heat. Start at 2 tsp and add more after tasting; the heat settles a little as the pachadi rests.

seg.5e0bf03c1b36.en: Green chilli: replace the chilli powder with 4–5 green chillies, fried with the dals.

seg.d7301a50c407.en: Onion-tomato: fry 1 sliced onion until soft before the tomatoes go in.

seg.bc90e2638112.en: Hotter: use 1 tsp Teja chilli powder in place of 1 tsp of the Sannam; Teja is very hot, so go slowly.

seg.aab608a427a9.en: Without garlic: leave out the garlic and add a pinch more asafoetida to the tempering.

seg.62d9491c4e58.en: Mix a spoonful into hot rice with a little ghee, or serve alongside dosa, idli, pesarattu or upma.

seg.3f0b892d2728.en: Keep it in a clean, dry glass jar in the fridge and eat within 4 days. Always use a dry spoon.

seg.20425f76c6e2.en: How do you make Andhra tomato pachadi?

seg.32ae9ac6b03c.en: Fry urad dal, chana dal and methi in oil, cook chopped tomatoes with turmeric and salt until the juice dries up, then grind everything coarsely with chilli powder, garlic and tamarind. Finish with a mustard, red chilli and curry-leaf tempering.

seg.2e87824684cb.en: Why is my tomato pachadi bitter?

seg.b367557bedfc.en: Usually the methi seeds burnt or there were too many. Use only ¼ tsp for 500 g tomatoes and fry them on medium-low heat, lifting them out as soon as they turn golden.

seg.acdf33e5cc6d.en: Can I make tomato pachadi without tamarind?

seg.53fbd8949e0b.en: Yes, if your tomatoes are sour enough. Taste after cooking; ripe, sweet tomatoes need the small piece of tamarind for balance.

seg.2938c7a0249e.en: How long does tomato pachadi last?

seg.a35105e3a4af.en: About 4 days in the fridge in a clean, dry jar, as long as the tomatoes were cooked down well and you use a dry spoon.

seg.3d323a4b41cc.en: Tomato pappu is the everyday dal of Andhra homes: toor dal (kandi pappu) cooked soft with tomatoes and green chillies, mashed smooth and finished with a garlic tempering. It is cooked most days of the week and eaten with hot rice, a spoon of ghee and an appadam or a pickle on the side.

seg.734276af9399.en: Our turmeric powder goes into the cooker with the dal and gives it a deep yellow colour. Sannam chilli powder adds a red tinge and a steady, medium heat that sits behind the sour tomato. This recipe serves 4.

seg.4efa92e0ce99.en: Wash the toor dal in 2–3 changes of water and drain it.

seg.3f536116a096.en: Put the dal in a pressure cooker with the tomatoes, green chillies, onion and 2½ cups of water.

seg.7d012f63f2a2.en: Pressure-cook the dal with the tomatoes, green chillies and turmeric powder for 4 whistles. Stir the turmeric powder into the water before closing the lid, then cook on medium heat.

seg.5dccba018dbc.en: Let the pressure drop on its own, about 10 minutes. The dal is done when a grain mashes completely between two fingers.

seg.da76f4c700ad.en: Mash well; add the chilli powder and salt. Use a wooden masher (pappu gutti) or the back of a ladle and mash while the dal is still hot, until the tomatoes and dal turn into one smooth mix.

seg.c1cb2443fbeb.en: Simmer 5 minutes with a splash of water. Add up to ½ cup water for a pouring consistency, and the tamarind water if using, and keep the heat on low so it does not catch.

seg.b24472a45a67.en: Taste for salt and sourness, then stir in the coriander leaves and switch off.

seg.6f90b7e4f66a.en: Heat the ghee in a small pan on medium heat and add the mustard seeds; let them splutter.

seg.0d1dd3c84a64.en: Fry mustard, cumin, garlic and curry leaves in the ghee; pour over. Add the cumin, garlic and dry red chillies after the mustard and fry until the garlic turns golden, then add the curry leaves and hing, and pour the sizzling tempering over the dal.

seg.81a1668adc10.en: Cover for 2 minutes so the tempering flavours the dal, then stir and serve hot.

seg.f904a5f14a1b.en: Mash the dal while it is hot for a smooth pappu. Once it cools, the grains set and stay lumpy.

seg.1a8211877e00.en: Sannam chilli powder is medium-hot. Start with 1 tsp; go up to 2 tsp for a spicier pappu.

seg.d85da2ea2cf7.en: Ripe, sour country tomatoes (natu tomatoes) give the best flavour; with mild hybrid tomatoes add the tamarind water.

seg.37f3ad1bf7b9.en: Let the garlic turn golden in the tempering before the curry leaves go in; pale garlic tastes raw.

seg.dfd3706fe457.en: Teja chilli powder: for a hotter pappu, use ½ tsp Teja chilli powder in place of the Sannam. Teja is very hot, so do not go over 1 tsp.

seg.434f1a510bbb.en: Palakura tomato pappu: add 2 cups chopped spinach to the dal after mashing and simmer 5 minutes.

seg.8d7a932afdbe.en: Pesarapappu: make it with yellow moong dal and cook for 2 whistles only.

seg.94f44314ecbb.en: Serve hot with steamed rice, a spoon of ghee and an appadam or avakaya on the side. It also goes well with chapati.

seg.29a23e2fa864.en: Keep leftovers covered in the fridge and eat within 2 days. The dal thickens when chilled; add a little hot water and heat through before serving.

seg.8e56f1d7c871.en: How many whistles for toor dal in a pressure cooker?

seg.562abdd39933.en: About 4 whistles on medium heat, then let the pressure drop on its own. Older dal or dal that was not washed well may need 5.

seg.6a800f643cf1.en: What is the difference between tomato pappu and sambar?

seg.05135ac52968.en: Tomato pappu is a thick, mashed dal with a simple tempering and no sambar powder or vegetables. Sambar is thinner, uses tamarind, vegetables and a roasted spice powder.

seg.19117f898a31.en: Can I make tomato pappu without a pressure cooker?

seg.631df239c7a7.en: Yes. Soak the dal for 30 minutes and cook it in a covered pot with 3½ cups of water for about 40–45 minutes, stirring now and then, until it mashes easily.

seg.b1140d6c02b4.en: Why is my tomato pappu too sour?

seg.6fb0505bf751.en: Some tomatoes are very sour. Simmer the dal a few more minutes and stir in a pinch of jaggery or a spoon of extra mashed dal to balance it.

seg.464f01dcf4e8.en: Vellulli kaaram is the garlic chilli podi kept on Andhra dining tables: red chilli powder pounded with plenty of garlic, roasted coriander and cumin, and salt. Mixed into the first handful of hot rice with ghee, or sprinkled over idli and dosa with a little oil, it is a quick meal on busy days and a staple in tiffin boxes.

seg.a9654adade5e.en: Our Teja chilli powder makes it deep red and very hot, the way Guntur homes like it. For less heat, use half Sannam chilli powder.

seg.074d39a3f8b1.en: Peel the garlic and pat the cloves completely dry with a cloth; any water shortens how long the podi keeps.

seg.33bb0e9eea87.en: Dry-roast the coriander and cumin seeds till fragrant; let them cool. Use a small pan on medium-low heat; this takes 1–2 minutes, and the coriander should turn a shade darker, not brown.

seg.a2f7a86fc993.en: Warm the garlic in 1 tsp oil for 2 minutes. Keep the heat low and stir; the cloves should soften slightly at the edges without browning. Let it cool.

seg.a4d0f7c87bd5.en: Grind the seeds to a powder, then pulse with the chilli powder and salt. Add the tamarind with the seeds, if using, so it breaks down evenly.

seg.c12763cab28c.en: Add the garlic and pulse in short bursts to a coarse, moist powder. Stop and scrape down the jar after every 2–3 pulses, as garlic sticks to the sides.

seg.31358182425b.en: In a stone mortar, pound the seeds first, then the garlic with the salt, and work in the chilli powder last.

seg.29ac6dd20660.en: Taste a pinch with a little rice and ghee, and add salt if needed.

seg.b4ccc3b591dd.en: Spread the podi on a plate for 10 minutes so the steam escapes, then pack it into a clean, dry jar.

seg.23d348ffe051.en: Teja is very hot; use half Sannam for a milder podi, or cut the chilli powder to 3 tbsp for the same garlic.

seg.948075d5f572.en: Dry the garlic well and warm it in oil; damp garlic makes the podi go off quickly.

seg.1a71c64c8c74.en: Pulse, do not run the mixer: run it long and the garlic turns into a paste.

seg.d1432fb9a627.en: Mix 1 tsp podi with 1 tsp ghee into a cup of hot rice; adjust to taste.

seg.bdc5e9728b98.en: With dals: dry-roast 1 tbsp chana dal and 1 tbsp urad dal with the seeds for a nuttier, slightly milder podi.

seg.767f9e16fa95.en: Raw garlic: skip warming the garlic for a sharper taste; keep it in the fridge and eat it within 3 days.

seg.21139bdcd961.en: Medium heat: use 2 tbsp Teja and 2 tbsp Sannam chilli powder.

seg.bceea7c8cb4f.en: Mix with the first handful of hot rice and ghee, or sprinkle over idli, dosa or pesarattu with a little oil or ghee.

seg.8665687f81ce.en: Keep in a clean, dry, airtight jar in the fridge and use it within 2 weeks. Always use a dry spoon.

seg.c58bc6538b2f.en: How do you make vellulli kaaram?

seg.0ecd3203de93.en: Roast coriander and cumin seeds, grind them, add chilli powder and salt, then pulse in peeled garlic cloves to a coarse, moist powder. Andhra homes often pound it in a stone mortar.

seg.727d415cb888.en: How do I make garlic podi less spicy?

seg.e4231ea5cf7a.en: Use half Sannam chilli powder in place of half the Teja, or use 3 tbsp chilli powder in all. Eating it with plenty of ghee also takes the edge off.

seg.982e854e4417.en: How long does vellulli kaaram last?

seg.367798df40e3.en: Up to 2 weeks in a dry, airtight jar in the fridge. Dry the garlic well and warm it in oil first, and always use a dry spoon.

seg.4c626acd1bdd.en: Can I use whole dried red chillies instead of chilli powder?

seg.1d41be2d17f9.en: Yes. Roast about 20 dried red chillies in a few drops of oil until crisp, cool and grind them before adding the garlic.

seg.d8082aa0cdf1.en: Cane jaggery or palm jaggery: which to use

seg.5094f960d9a4.en: Bellam in a Telugu kitchen usually means one of two things: cheruku bellam, made from sugarcane juice, or thati bellam, made from the sap of the palmyra palm. FSSAI treats them as two separate products, each with its own standard.

seg.13fd9611c493.en: They can look alike in a lump, but they taste different and suit different dishes. Here is how to tell them apart, which to use where, and how to keep them. There is a full Telugu section further down.

seg.70c115199d4c.en: Cane jaggery (cheruku bellam) is boiled-down sugarcane juice with a mellow, caramel sweetness: the one for payasam, pongal and chimmili. Palm jaggery (thati bellam) is boiled-down palmyra sap, darker and deeper in taste: a favourite in filter coffee and tea. You can swap one for the other gram for gram; start with a little less palm jaggery. Keep both in an airtight jar.

seg.cc5783126657.en: Is palm jaggery the same as karupatti?

seg.f7071649dddd.en: Yes. Karupatti is the Tamil name for jaggery made from palmyra sap. In Telugu it is thati bellam, and in Hindi taad ka gud.

seg.a591ce90fac8.en: Is gud the same as jaggery?

seg.9e04d6270c92.en: Yes. Gud, or gur, is the Hindi word for jaggery, and bellam is the Telugu one. On its own it usually means cane jaggery.

seg.e531a25812a8.en: Why has my jaggery gone sticky?

seg.cc79285bfadd.en: It has taken in moisture from the air, which happens faster in humid weather. Move it to an airtight jar and use a dry spoon.

seg.1bdcd09c5ca0.en: Can I use palm jaggery in payasam?

seg.8ba95d799ac9.en: Yes. It gives a darker colour and a deeper taste. Add it off the heat, as you would cane jaggery.

seg.1841c397898f.en: FSSAI's standard says chilli powder must be dry and free from dirt, added colouring matter, flavouring matter and mineral oil. Its testing manual has methods for finding brick powder, added starch, added colour, colours that dissolve in oil, and the dyes Sudan III and Rhodamine B.

seg.a0af610174e4.en: Some of this you can check in your kitchen with a glass of water, your fingers and a few drops of iodine. Some, like Sudan dyes, only a lab can find. This guide covers both. Try the checks on any chilli powder you buy.

seg.a574ced14407.en: Sprinkle a teaspoon of chilli powder on a glass of water and do not stir. Colour streaks running down at once point to added colour, and bits still floating after the powder sinks point to sawdust or bran. Rub the sediment: grit points to brick powder or sand, a soapy feel to soapstone. Iodine turning the powder blue points to added starch. Dyes such as Sudan I do not show in water; for those, use a lab.

seg.11caa5f871e4.en: What FSSAI checks chilli powder for

seg.7d346e39c41e.en: FSSAI's chilli powder standard does not allow added colouring matter. FSSAI's tests look for colours that dissolve in water, colours that dissolve in oil, and the dyes Sudan III and Rhodamine B.

seg.dab0f1b06607.en: Sudan I is used to colour oils, fats, waxes, and shoe and floor polish. The Indian Standard on quick tests for adulterants says Sudan III, much used in wax polishes, has been used to make chilli pods shine, and so finds its way into chilli powder.

seg.65d2132b3a71.en: Brick powder, sand, salt, talc and soapstone

seg.eaaa28049f76.en: FSSAI's household tests list these for chilli powder. The Indian Standard says brick powder is mixed in to increase bulk.

seg.591f55c64be8.en: FSSAI's manual tests powdered spices other than turmeric for added starch. The Indian Standard notes that colour is also added to chilli powder to hide added starch.

seg.6cdabb4ac9cc.en: Both float on water, which is how FSSAI's household tests spot them.

seg.2ad2a1900226.en: Check 1: the water glass and the rub test

seg.1b1af7f63ffd.en: Fill a clear glass with water at room temperature.

seg.5ebb4d43f1c6.en: Sprinkle one teaspoon of chilli powder on top. Do not stir.

seg.e11be0844965.en: Watch the first minute. Look for coloured streaks running down from the powder.

seg.14ad43586f91.en: Leave it until most of the powder has sunk. Look at the surface for bits still floating.

seg.379262f468f1.en: Pour off most of the water and rub the sediment at the bottom between your fingers.

seg.9d20132af7ae.en: Colour streaks running down at once

seg.4dd6d7d4418f.en: Added colour that dissolves in water

seg.99d03e1725f4.en: Bits still floating after the powder sinks

seg.0778aeb79734.en: White sediment that feels soapy and smooth

seg.92ba3085667d.en: No sign of what this check can find.

seg.e4f5d2924afa.en: Possible adulteration. Stop using that batch and get it tested.

seg.e5e493d4cb12.en: ⟦1⟧Why it works.⟦/1⟧ Colours that dissolve in water leave the powder and run down as streaks. Brick powder is heavy and settles to the bottom, while sawdust and bran float.

seg.551c97147aa3.en: ⟦1⟧What it misses.⟦/1⟧ Dyes that do not dissolve in water stay in the powder. Sudan I is one: it does not dissolve in water, and it is used to colour oils, fats and waxes. Chilli powder coloured with such dyes can pass this check. Only a lab test can rule them out.

seg.3d76d0b2a476.en: FSSAI's manual uses the iodine test for powdered spices other than turmeric, so chilli powder can take it. ⟦1⟧Our turmeric guide⟦/1⟧ explains why turmeric is left out.

seg.c7d23b036696.en: Put half a teaspoon of chilli powder on a white saucer.

seg.9b2fb67a0f9a.en: Add a few drops of tincture of iodine from a chemist.

seg.2d93dfc80312.en: Look at the colour where the drops land.

seg.0db85a4ff58c.en: Points to added starch. Stop using that batch and get it tested. On red powder a faint change is hard to judge, so if you are not sure, let a lab decide.

seg.ed4a959013d8.en: ⟦1⟧Why it works.⟦/1⟧ Iodine turns blue when it meets starch.

seg.9e0f62706054.en: Acid and solvent tests at home

seg.f5e28e97055b.en: The methods in FSSAI's manual for brick powder, added colour, oil-soluble colours, Sudan III and Rhodamine B in chilli powder use strong acids and solvents such as chloroform, petroleum ether, hexane and acetone. The acids can cause burns, and several of the solvents catch fire easily. They belong in a lab, not a kitchen.

seg.1e30ce9ef855.en: For a sure answer, send a sample to a NABL-accredited food testing lab. Ask it to test for added colours, including Sudan dyes, and against FSSAI's chilli powder standard. Its limits include moisture up to 11%, total ash up to 8%, and ash insoluble in dilute hydrochloric acid up to 1.3%, all by weight, with both ash limits on a dry basis. Keep the powder in its sealed pack or a clean sealed bag, and note the batch number printed on the pack.

seg.456379c75c24.en: Read the pack before you buy

seg.8ef59aeeebe4.en: An FSSAI licence or registration number.

seg.476e4849c1d8.en: The name and address of whoever made or packed it.

seg.f90b0f258a47.en: Net quantity, a batch or lot number, and a best-before date.

seg.fa3907160dbb.en: The ingredients. FSSAI allows up to 2% edible vegetable oil by weight in chilli powder, but only if the label says which oil and how much.

seg.616cb55edf33.en: Where it was grown, and the chilli variety if named. Our ⟦1⟧Sannam⟦/1⟧ and ⟦2⟧Teja⟦/2⟧ packs say Palnadu and Guntur.

seg.7cdc58c0c7e8.en: Keep the pack zipped shut, or move the powder to a dry, airtight jar.

seg.5766b566dbba.en: Use a dry spoon, and keep the jar away from steam from the stove.

seg.ae76fa3c0a37.en: Keep it in a cool, dry place, out of direct sunlight.

seg.cee32139c40b.en: Use it within the best-before date on the pack, in dishes such as ⟦1⟧vellulli kaaram⟦/1⟧, ⟦2⟧gongura pachadi⟦/2⟧ or ⟦3⟧tomato pachadi⟦/3⟧.

seg.13c76694dc1e.en: How do I check chilli powder for brick powder at home?

seg.3e87e1d30613.en: Put a teaspoon of chilli powder in a glass of water and let it settle. Pour off most of the water and rub the sediment between your fingers: grit points to brick powder or sand, and a white residue that feels soapy and smooth points to soapstone.

seg.f609f5773557.en: Can the water test detect Sudan dye in chilli powder?

seg.7bd8af24de2f.en: No. Sudan I does not dissolve in water, so it cannot run out as streaks. FSSAI's manual tests for Sudan III and for oil-soluble colours with solvents such as hexane and petroleum ether, so those tests need a lab.

seg.d63c02ec2e5c.en: Does the iodine test work on chilli powder?

seg.01e86c518d41.en: Yes. FSSAI's manual uses the iodine test for powdered spices other than turmeric, and chilli powder is one of them. A blue colour points to added starch.

seg.75e20911cd47.en: Is bright red chilli powder a sign of adulteration?

seg.dcfec3eff0b8.en: Colour alone does not tell you. The water check looks for colour that leaves the powder and runs down as streaks, not for how red the powder looks, and a lab can test for added colours.

seg.87fe2929801d.en: What should I do if a check looks wrong?

seg.54f85d34859f.en: Stop using that batch and keep the pack. Contact the seller with the batch number, or send a sample to a NABL-accredited food testing lab for a sure answer.

seg.0e55b39feef1.en: Hill turmeric (konda pasupu) or turmeric: the difference

seg.ebf6f90777d6.note: text on /learn/hill-turmeric-vs-turmeric/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.8b7a90a6aed6.en: Konda pasupu means hill turmeric: turmeric grown in hill country. In Andhra Pradesh that includes the agency hills of the Eastern Ghats around Araku Valley, Chintapalle and Paderu, where most tribal farmers grow turmeric. Plains turmeric grows on farmland in districts such as Guntur.

seg.404d008584f4.en: FSSAI's standard for turmeric powder is the same wherever it grew. What changes is the place, the variety, and how it is grown and dried. This guide covers each of those, what curcumin is, how to cook with each and how to compare two turmerics fairly. There is a Telugu section further down.

seg.2e709bd87897.note: text on /learn/hill-turmeric-vs-turmeric/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.10eec083bb3d.en: Hill turmeric (konda pasupu) grows in hill country, such as the Eastern Ghats around Araku, where most tribal farmers grow it. Plains turmeric grows on farmland in districts such as Guntur. Both are boiled, dried and ground, and FSSAI holds both to the same standard. Curcumin, the yellow pigment in turmeric, changes with variety, soil, climate and processing, so the word hill or plains does not tell you how much a turmeric has. Cook with both the same way.

seg.34cc236d9133.en: Farmland in districts such as Guntur

seg.186488dd4390.en: ICAR-IISR's general guide: a well-managed crop is ready in 7 to 9 months, usually dug between January and March

seg.a5d9b319040e.en: Boiled and dried by hand, which takes a lot of labour and firewood

seg.9094d5bd4e83.en: The usual steps: boiled, sun-dried, then polished by hand or by machine

seg.d3963fd16edc.en: The same one for both: at least 2% curcuminoids on a dry basis, and added colour is not allowed

seg.2e323e56fef7.en: Araku and Maredumilli hills. Whole hill turmeric fingers, packed as fine powder

seg.ce4850eb3b73.en: Grown in Palnadu and Guntur. Sun-dried, stone-ground

seg.8c0d21f32664.en: The rows above describe each region in general, from the sources at the end of this page. Only the last row is about our packs.

seg.a9e5b44e1be6.en: ⟦1⟧Hill turmeric.⟦/1⟧ ICAR-IISR's report on the Paderu agency, the tribal hill country of the Eastern Ghats that takes in Araku Valley, Chintapalle and Paderu, says turmeric is grown there by most tribal farmers.
seg.a9e5b44e1be6.note: text on /learn/hill-turmeric-vs-turmeric/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.736e66a0b5de.en: ⟦1⟧Plains turmeric.⟦/1⟧ Guntur district lists turmeric among its commercial crops, with cotton, chillies and tobacco. Duggirala, in Guntur, has a turmeric processing cluster that makes processed turmeric and turmeric powder. In 2022, Guntur district was divided into three districts: Guntur, Palnadu and Bapatla.
seg.736e66a0b5de.note: text on /learn/hill-turmeric-vs-turmeric/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.0f26c0785ed1.en: Turmeric can be grown either way: ICAR-IISR says it can be grown rain-fed or irrigated, from sea level up to 1,500 m.

seg.b687346df428.en: Our ⟦1⟧hill turmeric⟦/1⟧ comes from the Araku and Maredumilli hills, and our ⟦2⟧turmeric⟦/2⟧ is grown in Palnadu and Guntur. Both are packed in Narasaraopet.
seg.b687346df428.note: text on /learn/hill-turmeric-vs-turmeric/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.9a5af9e957e1.en: How each is grown and dried

seg.e641ce21ee35.en: ⟦1⟧In the hills.⟦/1⟧ ICAR-IISR's Paderu report says tribal farmers there have grown a local variety called Chayapasupu, or Chintapalle Local, for ages. It has been common practice to leave it in the ground for two or three seasons, up to 18 to 24 months, before digging. From 2011-12, ICAR-IISR and the Horticultural Research Station at Chintapalle tested varieties for the hill zone and brought in Roma and IISR Pragati, which are dug after one season. The report says tribal farmers boil and dry their turmeric by hand, which takes a lot of labour and firewood; the project gave four farmer producer organisations turmeric boilers and polishers.
seg.e641ce21ee35.note: text on /learn/hill-turmeric-vs-turmeric/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.f93b2805162b.en: ⟦1⟧The usual steps.⟦/1⟧ ICAR-IISR's turmeric guide describes how the crop is handled after it is dug:
seg.f93b2805162b.note: text on /learn/hill-turmeric-vs-turmeric/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.675a9ec4355c.en: Dig it when the leaves dry and turn light brown to yellowish. A well-managed crop is ready seven to nine months after planting, usually between January and March.

seg.763940881dcd.en: Separate the fingers from the bulbs and boil them within 3 or 4 days of digging, in water until soft: 45 to 60 minutes for fingers and 90 minutes for bulbs. Boiling takes away the raw smell, cuts the drying time and gives an even colour.

seg.a52a5947071a.en: Dry them in the sun in layers 5 to 7 cm deep, heaped and covered at night. It may take 10 to 12 days for the moisture to fall below 12%.

seg.69d24ab1420a.en: Polish off the rough, dull, scaly skin by rubbing, by hand or in a turning drum.

seg.1b7d7df8b7fa.en: Grind the dried turmeric into powder. FSSAI allows turmeric powder up to 10% moisture.

seg.1668650874a7.en: Fingers are the side branches of the turmeric rhizome, usually 2.5 to 7.5 cm long; bulbs are the shorter, thicker central rhizome. Our hill turmeric pack says whole hill turmeric fingers, packed as fine powder. Our turmeric pack says sun-dried and stone-ground.

seg.7ef4d7667b4e.en: Curcumin is the yellow pigment in turmeric, ICAR-IISR says. FSSAI measures a turmeric powder's colouring power as its curcuminoid content, and asks for at least 2% on a dry basis. That standard is the same for hill and plains turmeric.

seg.fec370db2315.en: Curcumin changes from one turmeric to the next:

seg.bf314e75200d.en: ⟦1⟧Variety.⟦/1⟧ ICAR-IISR's 2022 turmeric guide lists its own varieties from 4.3% curcumin (Suvarna) to 6.5% (IISR Prabha).
seg.bf314e75200d.note: text on /learn/hill-turmeric-vs-turmeric/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.cee7632d2998.en: ⟦1⟧Soil and climate.⟦/1⟧ ICAR-IISR notes that turmeric from different regions differs in quality because of soil, climate and farming practice. Its Paderu report calls curcumin content highly sensitive to changes in the growing environment.
seg.cee7632d2998.note: text on /learn/hill-turmeric-vs-turmeric/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.70b529fe0f69.en: ⟦1⟧Processing.⟦/1⟧ Handling and processing after harvest add to the differences, and boiling too long or too short affects the quality of the dried turmeric.
seg.70b529fe0f69.note: text on /learn/hill-turmeric-vs-turmeric/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.493187b22749.en: So the word hill or plains on a pack does not tell you a turmeric's curcumin content. A food testing lab can measure the curcuminoid content of a batch.

seg.53dc21b97510.en: ⟦1⟧How they look.⟦/1⟧ Colour varies too. ICAR-IISR describes its varieties' rhizomes as ranging from reddish yellow to deep orange. Processing counts as well: boiling evens out the colour, drying in too thin a layer can spoil it, and polishing by hand leaves a rough, dull surface.
seg.53dc21b97510.note: text on /learn/hill-turmeric-vs-turmeric/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.d8ece11f902a.en: Cooking with each, and keeping it

seg.276f633c7a1f.en: Use either one wherever you use turmeric: dal, sambar, rasam, curries and pulihora.

seg.ca5e9b6340f2.en: Add it on a low flame so it does not burn.

seg.7e910d4ad2a1.en: To swap one for the other, start with the amount you usually use and adjust to taste.

seg.731001f6177d.en: Try either one in ⟦1⟧pasupu annam⟦/1⟧, ⟦2⟧nimmakaya pulihora⟦/2⟧, ⟦3⟧tomato pappu⟦/3⟧ or ⟦4⟧pasupu paalu⟦/4⟧.
seg.731001f6177d.note: text on /learn/hill-turmeric-vs-turmeric/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.073f63fe23e0.en: Use a dry spoon every time.

seg.b334ade49a15.en: Store it in a cool, dry place, away from light.

seg.ea935ed7c1aa.en: How to compare two turmerics fairly

seg.dcebc75ff722.en: Compare powder with powder. FSSAI allows whole turmeric up to 12% moisture and powder up to 10%, so the two are held to different limits.

seg.9d14be920107.en: Read both packs: where it was grown, the batch or lot number, the best-before date and the FSSAI licence or registration number. Note the batch numbers, so you know which lots you compared.

seg.fbb64b2b32b0.en: Do the water check on both, side by side, with the same amount in the same kind of glass. The steps are in ⟦1⟧how to check turmeric powder at home⟦/1⟧.
seg.fbb64b2b32b0.note: text on /learn/hill-turmeric-vs-turmeric/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.bd82039194f2.en: Cook the same dish with each, with the same amount, and compare the colour and taste.

seg.8949107c3ad8.en: Do not judge curcumin by colour alone. A brighter yellow is not a measurement; a food testing lab can measure curcuminoid content.

seg.1810d213ce3f.en: Konda pasupu is Telugu for hill turmeric: turmeric grown in hill country. In Andhra Pradesh it grows in the Eastern Ghats, for example in the Paderu agency around Araku Valley and Chintapalle, where most tribal farmers grow turmeric.

seg.15730f8cc6b8.en: Is hill turmeric different from regular turmeric?

seg.47cf644d0819.en: FSSAI holds all turmeric powder to the same standard, wherever it grew. Hill and plains turmeric can differ in where they grow, the varieties grown, and how they are grown and dried. In the Paderu hills, for example, an old local variety has often been left in the ground for up to two years.

seg.925655ca4b05.en: Does hill turmeric have more curcumin?

seg.0d1b42a32899.en: The word hill alone does not tell you. Curcumin changes with the variety, the soil and climate, and how the turmeric was boiled and dried. A food testing lab can measure the curcuminoid content of a batch.

seg.4bce9a44c11e.en: What are the types of turmeric (haldi) in India?

seg.4e6e7201dae6.en: ICAR-IISR says India grows many turmeric cultivars, mostly known by the name of the place where they are grown, such as Duggirala, Mydukur, Tekkurpet and Amalapuram. It has also released improved varieties such as IISR Prabha, IISR Prathibha and IISR Pragati.

seg.7f1a5999ea66.en: Can I use hill turmeric instead of regular turmeric?

seg.4ed419c2136a.en: Yes. Use it wherever you use turmeric, start with the amount you usually use, and add it on a low flame so it does not burn.

seg.1a441b0df6de.en: Both packs list one ingredient, turmeric (Curcuma longa), and name where it was grown.

seg.abda31761e23.en: Plain answers to what buyers ask us, starting with how to check turmeric powder at home.

seg.4bddab09b9f2.note: text on /learn/turmeric-adulteration-test/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.2b6b229e651e.en: FSSAI's standard says turmeric powder must be free from added colouring matter, including lead chromate, and from foreign starch. Its testing manual lists what inspectors check turmeric for: added dyes such as metanil yellow, lead salts, and chalk powder.

seg.b27088069a9d.en: Some of this you can check in your kitchen, and some only a lab can find. This guide covers both, plus two popular tests that do not work for turmeric. Try them on any turmeric you buy, ours included.

seg.b74ab3f9bb3e.en: Two glasses of water after the turmeric check. Left: pale yellow water with the powder settled at the bottom. Right: strong yellow water with yellow trails running down from the powder.

seg.c8b6eb5f9530.en: ⟦1⟧The water check⟦/1⟧Left: the powder has settled and the water is pale yellow. Right: strong yellow trails ran from the powder as it sank, and the water turned deep yellow. That one is worth a lab test.
seg.c8b6eb5f9530.note: text on /learn/turmeric-adulteration-test/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.a7363cc3fa37.en: Sprinkle a teaspoon of turmeric on a glass of water and let it settle without stirring. Turmeric sinks and leaves the water pale yellow; water that turns strong yellow straight away points to added colour. This check cannot find lead chromate or chalk, so for a sure answer, use a food testing lab. Skip the iodine test: turmeric is starchy to begin with.

seg.34d6f989bfaf.en: Such as metanil yellow, which can make dull turmeric look brighter. FSSAI does not allow added colour in turmeric.

seg.042cabe54b01.en: Lead chromate and other lead salts

seg.8310b11eab8b.en: Lead chromate is a yellow pigment used in paint. Stanford-led studies published in 2019 and 2024 found it in turmeric from parts of South Asia. FSSAI does not allow it in turmeric at all.

seg.4278e7c5416c.en: A cheap white powder that adds weight.

seg.5a8b446bbce0.en: Flour or starch from other crops. FSSAI's standard rules it out too.

seg.653731f2ed6f.en: Sprinkle one level teaspoon of turmeric powder on top. Do not stir.

seg.ea5b43cf8436.en: Watch the first minute as the powder sinks. Look for coloured trails running down from it.

seg.e37698aaa3fb.en: Leave it for 15 to 20 minutes. Then hold the glass against a white wall or a sheet of paper and look at the water above the settled powder.

seg.e8937cebf136.en: Pale yellow water, powder at the bottom

seg.256ce5cf303d.en: Strong yellow trails, or deep yellow water within minutes

seg.ce06c8148072.en: Possible added colour. Stop using that batch and get it tested.

seg.53d9c5db264d.en: ⟦1⟧Why it works.⟦/1⟧ Turmeric's own yellow, curcumin, hardly dissolves in water, so the powder sinks and only tints the water. Dyes such as metanil yellow dissolve easily and colour the water fast.
seg.53d9c5db264d.note: text on /learn/turmeric-adulteration-test/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.af4442c6e910.en: ⟦1⟧What it misses.⟦/1⟧ Lead chromate and chalk do not dissolve in water either, so turmeric mixed with them can pass this check. Only a lab test can rule them out.
seg.af4442c6e910.note: text on /learn/turmeric-adulteration-test/; keep every ⟦n⟧ ⟦/n⟧ ⟦#n⟧ marker, around the matching words

seg.a8b61850b87d.en: Very fine powder can keep the water cloudy for a while. Cloudy is fine; a clear, strong yellow is what to look for.

seg.c3455d1f4c96.en: Check 2: if you buy whole turmeric

seg.3d4e366bb488.en: Snap a finger of dried turmeric in half. Turmeric is yellow-orange right through, so the inside should look much like the outside. A bright yellow skin over a pale or dull core can mean colour was added to the surface. Ask the seller about it, or get it tested.

seg.4c4dc95561d2.en: Iodine turns blue-black when it meets starch, and it is often suggested for spotting flour in turmeric. But turmeric is starchy itself, so it turns blue-black either way. That is why FSSAI's own manual uses the iodine test for powdered spices other than turmeric.

seg.fc16ff8016e3.en: FSSAI's tests for lead, metanil yellow and chalk in turmeric use concentrated hydrochloric or sulphuric acid. These acids burn skin and eyes. They belong in a lab, not a kitchen.

seg.1dd87aa7bdc7.en: For a sure answer: a food testing lab

seg.1883beca4d73.en: A NABL-accredited food testing lab can test turmeric for lead and for added colours. Ask the lab how much sample it needs, keep the powder in its sealed pack or a clean sealed bag, and note the batch number printed on the pack. FSSAI publishes a list of notified food testing labs on its website.

seg.ff7951e2f36b.en: An FSSAI licence or registration number. You can look it up on FSSAI's FoSCoS website.

seg.beee8eda6466.en: Net quantity, MRP, a batch or lot number, and a best-before date.

seg.f9270fd96202.en: Where it was grown. Turmeric from different regions differs in colour, so a named region helps you compare like with like.

seg.bb4d61f86b55.en: Use a dry spoon. A damp spoon is what makes turmeric lumpy.

seg.a92c022ff52e.en: Keep it out of direct sunlight, which fades the colour.

seg.6911ce63edde.en: Is very bright yellow turmeric a bad sign?

seg.a0ce62cee740.en: Not by itself. Colour changes with the variety, where it was grown and how it was dried and ground, so turmerics differ a lot. What matters is colour that leaves the powder too easily, as in the water check.

seg.e8cc5edbb092.en: Can the water check show that turmeric has no lead?

seg.37eb38df9ce8.en: No. Lead chromate does not dissolve in water, so the water check cannot see it. Only a lab test can.

seg.2b76cd3e665b.en: Moisture. A wet spoon or an open pack lets the powder take in water. Break the lumps with a dry spoon and keep the pack sealed.

seg.e83aba6cc6df.en: Stop using that batch, keep the pack, and contact the seller with the batch number. You can also report it to FSSAI through its Food Safety Connect app. If it is ours, WhatsApp us a photo of the pack and the glass.

seg.1dd4194330b1.en: Try these checks on ours too. If anything looks off, ⟦1⟧WhatsApp us⟦/1⟧ a photo with the batch number from the pack.
